usage_en: Used to list two or more actions or states when either one is possible.

examples.en: On weekends I watch movies or read books.
If you're tired or sick, take a rest.
I take the bus or walk.

compare: Use ~(이)나 to link nouns (커피나 차), and -거나 to link verbs or adjectives.

usage_en: Used to add a reason after your main point, as a soft explanation the listener didn't know.

examples.en: I can't go today — I have plans.
He's famous. He's a singer, you see.
I'll be a little late; I just left.

compare: With -어서 or -으니까 the reason comes first. With -거든요 the reason comes after your point.

usage_en: Used when a situation changes by circumstance rather than by your own decision.

examples.en: I ended up living in Korea.
I've come to like spicy food.
We happened to meet.

compare: -어지다 describes a state changing (예뻐지다). -게 되다 describes a situation changing.

usage_en: Used for a guess you make on the spot, or to state your intention politely.

examples.en: It'll probably rain tomorrow.
Wow, that looks delicious!
I'll do it.

compare: -을 거예요 is for a plan already decided. -겠- is for a thought you just had.

usage_en: Used when something finally happens, usually with regret, or to show firm determination.

examples.en: I ended up crying.
I ended up losing my wallet.
This time I'll succeed no matter what.

usage_en: Used to show that the first action was completed before the second one began.

examples.en: I went out after eating.
I got angry after hearing that.
I felt better after apologizing.

compare: -고 can simply list actions. -고서 makes clear the first action finished first.

usage_en: Used to state the purpose or goal of an action.

examples.en: I came in order to learn Korean.
I walk every day for my health.
I'm working hard to achieve my dream.

compare: -으려고 sounds conversational; -기 위해 sounds more formal or written.

usage_en: Used to say you have decided on something, or to make an agreement with others.

examples.en: I decided to start exercising tomorrow.
Let's agree to meet next week.
I decided to cut back on coffee.

usage_en: Used to give a reason based on something you observed or judged.

examples.en: Since the weather was nice, I took a walk.
It looked good, so I bought it.
I took a taxi since I had no time.

compare: -기에 is more written than -어서, and fits well when your reason is something you saw.

usage_en: Used to guess about something based on evidence you can see or hear.

examples.en: There must be a lot of people.
It seems to be raining outside.
That shop must be famous.

compare: -는 것 같다 is your personal impression. -나 보다 is a guess from visible evidence.

usage_en: Used to express a tentative thought or mild doubt about something.

examples.en: I wonder if it's too late.
I think maybe I made a mistake.
I'm not sure if this is right.

usage_en: Used when something you were doing prevented you from doing something else.

examples.en: I couldn't call because I was working.
I stayed up all night studying.

examples.ko: 드라마 보느라고 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어요.
examples.en: I lost track of time watching a drama.

compare: 비가 와서 못 갔어요 blames an outside cause. 자느라고 못 갔어요 blames what you yourself were doing.

usage_en: Used to soften an opinion when you are not fully sure.

examples.en: It kind of seems right.
It also seems a little difficult.

examples.ko: 괜찮은 것 같기도 한데 잘 모르겠어요.
examples.en: It might be fine, but I'm not sure.

usage_en: Used to correct a misunderstanding and give the real reason.

examples.en: It's not that I dislike it, it's just a bit much.

examples.ko: 못하는 게 아니라 안 하는 거예요.
examples.en: It's not that I can't — I just don't.
I'm not angry, just tired.

usage_en: Used to add a second action you can do conveniently while doing the first.

examples.ko: 나가는 김에 우유 좀 사 올게요.
examples.en: While I'm out, I'll grab some milk.
Since you're here, let's have some tea.
While cleaning, I organized too.

usage_en: Used to say something will happen right after another thing, or to do exactly as told.

examples.en: I'll call as soon as I arrive.
I said it just as I heard it.
I'll go as soon as it's over.

compare: -자마자 means instantly. -는 대로 means as soon as the condition is met, often about plans.

usage_en: Used to replace one thing with another, or to offer something in exchange.

examples.en: I ate bread instead of rice.
Instead of going out, I rested at home.

examples.ko: 제가 도와드리는 대신에 커피 사 주세요.
examples.en: I'll help you — in return, buy me a coffee.

usage_en: Used when an unexpected event caused a bad or unintended result.

examples.en: I was late because I overslept.
I couldn't go because it rained.
Things blew up because I posted that photo.

compare: -어서 is neutral. -는 바람에 implies the cause was unexpected and the result unwanted.

usage_en: Used when you believed something that turned out not to be true.

examples.en: I thought it was today.
I thought you were angry.
I thought you were Korean.

usage_en: Used to describe a general tendency without stating it too strongly.

examples.en: I'm on the quiet side.
I'm pretty good with spicy food.
This shop is relatively cheap.

usage_en: Used to report what someone else said or what you heard.

examples.en: Jisu said she's coming tomorrow.
I heard this place is good.
He said he's busy these days.

usage_en: Used to check something you heard about the listener.

examples.en: I heard you're learning Korean?
I heard you're going next week?
I heard that movie is good?

usage_en: Used to put a question inside a larger sentence.

examples.en: Do you know where it is?
I don't know whether it's right.
I asked why that is.

usage_en: Used to ask a question in a warm, casual way, often to someone younger or close to you.

examples.en: Did you eat?
Where are you going?
Are you okay?

compare: -어? is plain casual. -니? sounds gentler or more caring.

literal_en: as you know; as you can see
usage_en: Used when the listener already knows or can see what you are saying.

examples.en: As you know, today is a day off.
As you can see, it's crowded.
As I mentioned, there's no time.

usage_en: Used to report something you personally observed and found notable.

examples.en: It was bigger than I expected.
Korean food was spicy, I found.
There really were a lot of people.

compare: -더라 is casual and -더군요 is polite, but both report what you saw yourself.

usage_en: Used to tell a friend about something you experienced yourself.

examples.en: That cafe was really pretty.
It was easier than I thought.
There were tons of people.

usage_en: Used to suppose something that has not happened yet, and say it won't change the result.

examples.en: Even if it's hard, don't give up.
I'll go even if it rains.
Come even if you're late.

compare: -어도 works for real situations. -더라도 is stronger and used for things that haven't happened.

usage_en: Used to describe something you did repeatedly in the past or left unfinished.

examples.en: It's a cafe I used to go to often.
Please finish what you were eating.
It's the neighborhood I used to live in.

usage_en: Used to mention something you saw and leave the response to the listener.

examples.en: Someone was looking for you earlier.
It was cold out — take a jacket.
It was good — give it a try.

literal_en: so that; to the point of
usage_en: Used to state a purpose, or to show the extent something reaches.

examples.en: I left early so I wouldn't be late.
I wrote it big so it's easy to see.
I sang until my throat hurt.

compare: -게 is similar but shorter and more casual; -도록 sounds a little more formal.

usage_en: Used to ask a question in formal settings such as service, announcements, or interviews.

examples.en: Would you like to order?
Where are you from?
Is this time all right for you?

compare: Everyday conversation uses -어요?. Service, announcements and interviews use -습니까?.

usage_en: Used to make statements in formal settings such as introductions, presentations, or work.

examples.en: Nice to meet you.
I'm from the United States.
Thank you.

compare: Use -어요 with friends. Use -습니다 for introductions, announcements and the workplace.

usage_en: Used to talk about something that already happened.

examples.en: I met a friend yesterday.
I ate.
It was fun.

usage_en: Used when something is gradually progressing toward a point in the future.

examples.en: It's almost done.
The day is breaking.
I'm slowly getting used to it.

compare: -어 가다 looks forward from now. -어 오다 looks back at what you have done until now.

literal_en: do in advance and leave it
usage_en: Used when you finish something ahead of time and leave it in that state.

examples.en: I'll order it in advance.
I left the window open.
I've got all the ingredients ready.

compare: -어 두다 means almost the same thing; -어 놓다 sounds slightly more conversational.

usage_en: Used when you do something now and keep the result for later use.

examples.en: I saved the contact.
I saved us a seat.
I took a photo to keep.

usage_en: Used to offer to do something for a customer or someone older or senior.

examples.en: Let me help you.
Shall I take a photo for you?
I'll show you to your seat.

compare: -어 주다 is for friends and equals. -어 드리다 is the humble form for seniors and customers.

usage_en: Used when an action is finished off entirely, with relief or regret.

examples.en: I ate it all up.
I burned it.
I forgot.

compare: -고 말다 is similar, but -어 버리다 feels either more relieved or more regretful.

usage_en: Used to suggest trying something, or to say you have experienced it.

examples.en: Try eating it.
May I try it on?
I've been to Korea.

usage_en: Used for something you have continued doing from the past up to the present.

examples.en: I've been learning Korean for three years.
I've kept at it steadily.
It's the time we've walked together.

usage_en: Used to describe the state that remains after an action is finished.

examples.en: The flowers are in bloom.
The door is open.
I'm sitting in my seat.

compare: -고 있다 is the action in progress (옷을 입고 있다 = putting it on). -어 있다 is the resulting state (앉아 있다 = seated).

usage_en: Used when you do something for another person's benefit, or ask them to.

examples.en: I'll take a photo for you.
Could you help me a bit?
Please speak slowly.

usage_en: Used to give a reason, or to connect two actions in order.

examples.en: I ate because I was hungry.
Sorry I'm late.
I went to a cafe and studied.

compare: -어서 cannot be used before a command or suggestion. Say 늦었으니까 서두르세요, not 늦어서 서두르세요.

usage_en: Used for a decision you have just made about what you need to do.

examples.en: I should go to bed now.
I'd better pay more attention.
I should start exercising tomorrow.

usage_en: Used when a state gradually changes into another state.

examples.en: Korean has gotten easier.
The weather has gotten warm.
We've gotten a lot closer.

usage_en: Used to give a reason, especially before a command, suggestion, or invitation.

examples.en: Take an umbrella since it's raining.
Let's hurry since there's no time.
It's good, so give it a try.

compare: Use -어서 for apologies and thanks. Use -으니까 before commands and suggestions.

usage_en: Used when you move somewhere with a purpose.

examples.en: Let's go eat.
I came to meet a friend.
I went to the bookstore to buy a book.

compare: Only 가다, 오다 and 다니다 can follow -으러. For other verbs use -으려고.

usage_en: Used to say something is not allowed or not advisable.

examples.en: You mustn't take photos here.
You shouldn't overdo it.
You can't throw this away here.

compare: This is the opposite of -어도 되다 (permission), and sounds softer than -지 마세요.

usage_en: Used when one person does two things at the same time.

examples.en: I walk while listening to music.
We talked over coffee.
She said it with a smile.

usage_en: Used for polite instructions in announcements, notices, and customer service.

examples.en: Please wait a moment.
Please stand behind the safety line.
Please have a seat.

compare: Everyday speech uses -으세요. Announcements and service settings use -으십시오.

usage_en: Used to say one action happens after another is finished.

examples.en: After washing my face, I put on lotion.
I'll go after I eat.
I'll let you know after checking.

usage_en: Used to say how much time has passed since something happened.

examples.en: It's been six months since I came to Korea.
I haven't been learning long.
It's been a long time since we met.

compare: Only 되다, 지나다 and 넘다 follow -은 지. For 'know whether', use -는지 instead.

usage_en: Used to put two events in order, with the first one finished.

examples.en: Let's meet after class.
I took a walk after eating.
I'll tell you after I think about it.

usage_en: Used for a plan you have already decided, or a prediction about the future.

examples.en: I'll go tomorrow.
It'll probably rain.
I'm going to keep studying.

compare: -겠어요 is a thought you just had. -을 거예요 is a plan already made.

usage_en: Used when something happens without fail on each occasion.

examples.en: Every time I come here, I feel good.
Every time I hear this song, I think of it.
It looks pretty every time I see it.

usage_en: Used when there is no other option, or when a result is completely natural.

examples.en: I had no choice but to wait.

examples.ko: 이 맛이면 줄 설 수밖에 없어요.
examples.en: With this taste, you have to queue.
Of course you'd be upset.

usage_en: Used to state your own intention and then ask or suggest something.

examples.en: I'll do it, so don't worry.
I'll wait, so take your time.
I'll get it ready, so please wait a moment.

usage_en: Used to guess about someone's situation while showing concern or regret.

examples.en: It must be hard — are you okay?
Thank you for coming though you must be busy.
It'll be cold — take a jacket.

usage_en: Used for a casual guess, or to express regret about something you didn't do.

examples.en: It's probably closed.
I should have said something then.
I should have booked in advance.

usage_en: Used to promise the listener that you will do something.

examples.en: I'll do it.
I'll call you later.
I'll head out first.

compare: -을 거야 is just your plan. -을게 is a promise made to the listener, so it needs someone to hear it.

usage_en: Used to suggest doing something together or to offer to do something.

examples.en: Shall we go together?
Shall I help you?
What shall we eat?

usage_en: Used when one thing increases as another increases.

examples.en: The more I eat, the better it tastes.
The more you practice, the better you get.
The more I learn, the harder it gets.

compare: Often used together as -으면 -을수록, as in 보면 볼수록.

usage_en: Used to suggest doing something together in a formal or group setting.

examples.en: Let's toast!
Let's go together.
Let's begin now.

compare: Avoid this with people senior to you; use -으실래요? or -으시죠 instead.

usage_en: Used when the second action happens immediately after the first.

examples.en: I'll go as soon as class ends.
I called as soon as I arrived.
I knew the moment I saw it.

compare: -는 대로 is often about plans. -자마자 stresses that it happened instantly.

usage_en: Used to remind the listener of something you both already know.

examples.en: I told you yesterday, remember?
We used to come here a lot.
You like it too, don't you?

usage_en: Used to contrast two ideas in one sentence.

examples.en: It's hard but fun.
It was spicy but delicious.
I don't have time, but I want to go.

usage_en: Used to join two nouns or to say you did something together with someone.

examples.en: I ate kimchi and rice.
I went with a friend.
Korea and France are different.

compare: ~과/와 is used in writing and formal speech; ~하고 and ~(이)랑 are conversational.

usage_en: Used when giving or saying something to someone you should show respect to.

examples.en: I gave it to my teacher.
I wrote a letter to my parents.
I'll tell the boss.

compare: ~께 is the honorific form of ~에게 and ~한테.

usage_en: Used to mark the subject when that person deserves respect.

examples.en: The teacher has arrived.
My grandmother made it.
The boss is calling for you.

compare: ~께서 is the honorific form of ~이/가, and the verb usually takes -으시- as well.

usage_en: Used to say something applies to each and every one, without exception.

examples.en: I hike every weekend.
Culture differs from country to country.
Everyone has their own taste.

usage_en: Used to limit something to one thing and nothing else.

examples.en: Just water, please.
Just a little, please.
I was the only one who didn't know.

usage_en: Used to say two things are about the same in degree or amount.

examples.en: It's not as hard as I thought.
I improved as much as I worked at it.
You speak as well as a Korean.

compare: ~보다 points out a difference. ~만큼 says the degree is the same.

usage_en: Used to say there is nothing more than this; always followed by a negative.

examples.en: I only have a thousand won.
Only one person came.
This is all I can do.

compare: ~만 takes a positive verb (물만 주세요). ~밖에 must be followed by a negative.

usage_en: Used to mark the starting point and the end point of time or place.

examples.en: I work from 9 to 6.
I'm going from Seoul to Busan.
I watched it from start to finish.

usage_en: Used to say that is the whole of it and there is nothing else.

examples.en: You're the only one I can trust.
It's only once.
I just smiled, that's all.

usage_en: Used to mark the person who receives something or is spoken to.

examples.en: I gave a gift to my friend.
Ask me.
I told my younger sibling.

compare: ~에게 is written, ~한테 is spoken. Both are only for people and animals; use ~에 for places.

usage_en: Used to emphasize the starting point of a movement or process.

examples.en: I walked starting from here.
I came all the way from Seoul.
Let's start over from the very beginning.

usage_en: Used to mark a direction, a means of doing something, or a material.

examples.en: I go by subway.
Go to the right.
This is made with beans.

usage_en: Used to casually ask what the other person wants to do.

examples.en: Would you like to go together?
What would you like to drink?
Want to sing a song?

compare: -을까요? proposes doing it together. -을래요? asks what the listener wants.

usage_en: Used when something is not enough but is still better than nothing.

examples.en: I rested, if only briefly.
I want to help, even if only a little.
Please take this, small as it is.

usage_en: Used to raise a topic or to define what something really is.

examples.en: What is happiness, anyway?
That's what friends are for.
Korean is really interesting.

usage_en: Used to say what something or someone is; the most basic way to make a statement.

examples.en: I'm a student.
This is yuja tea.
My name is Emma.

compare: Use 이에요 after a final consonant (학생이에요) and 예요 after a vowel (차예요).

usage_en: Used to compare something to another thing it resembles.

examples.en: You speak like a Korean.
It's pretty like a petal.
Let's meet like yesterday.

compare: ~같이 means almost the same; ~처럼 sounds slightly more written.

usage_en: Used to say that not only the bigger thing but even the smaller thing was impossible.

examples.en: Far from traveling, I don't even have time to rest.
Instead of praise, I got scolded.
I couldn't even drink water, let alone eat.

usage_en: Used in everyday speech to join nouns or to say you did something with someone.

examples.en: Tteokbokki and sundae, please.
I went with a friend.
Come with me.

usage_en: Used to mark the person something was received or heard from.

examples.en: I heard it from a friend.
I got it from my older sister.
Who did you learn it from?

compare: ~에게서 is written, ~한테서 is spoken. Use these when the person is the source.
